Last Generation Theology

A Bible handbook study

Thesis. Man is dust made alive by the breath of God — a living soul, whole and mortal (Gen. 2:7). Sin is not a guilt inherited at birth but the consented transgression of the law (1 John 3:4; Jas. 1:14-15); yet the fallen nature we do inherit corrupts and enslaves (Rom. 7:14; Eph. 2:3). Into that very flesh the Son of God came — the second Adam, bearing the full fallen nature of man after four thousand years of sin, yet without sin (Rom. 8:3; Heb. 2:14-17; 4:15) — conceived of the Spirit and living from the manger, by faith in His Father, the surrendered life we enter by the new birth of water and the Spirit (John 3:5). Salvation is God saving His people FROM their sins, not in them (Matt. 1:21): righteousness by faith — the gospel in verity, the third angel’s message in verity — both credits Christ’s obedience to the believer and works it in him, so that complete victory over sin is provided, promised, and expected (Rom. 6:14; 1 John 5:4; Jude 24; Rev. 3:21). That message ripens a last generation who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus (Rev. 14:12), stand through the time of trouble without a mediator because their sins have gone beforehand to judgment (Rev. 22:11; Dan. 12:1), and in whom the character of Christ is perfectly reproduced — the harvest that vindicates God before the universe (Mark 4:29; Rev. 14:1-5).

Method. After Haskell's Bible Handbook: ref → gloss, scannable; every doctrine established first from Scripture (Miller's Rule — the Bible defines its own terms), then corroborated by a central cloud of witnesses — E. J. Waggoner, A. T. Jones, S. N. Haskell, and Ellen G. White — quoted VERBATIM and verified against the corpus. This study argues the historic Adventist “last generation” understanding: full victory over sin through the indwelling Christ. On the nature of Christ it is careful and honest: He took our fallen NATURE, never our sin — nature is not guilt, and sin is in the consent — so no line may make Christ a sinner, and no line may give Him an unfallen-Adam advantage. Where a source cannot be quoted from the local corpus, the point rests on Scripture and what CAN be verified; no claim without a receipt.

Part I — The Man

¶1. Dust and Breath — What Man Is

Dust of the ground plus the breath of God equals a living soul — man does not HAVE a soul, he IS one: a single, undivided, mortal being; and everything this handbook says about sin and salvation happens in that one whole man.

Dust + breath = a living soul — Gen. 2:7; 1 Cor. 15:45:

  • Gen. 2:7. "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." — the master text: two components, one result; man does not receive a soul, man BECOMES one — the soul is the sum, not an occupant.
    • the living soul = the WHOLE man himself — the sum produced when God joined dust (the body) to the breath of life; not a part inside man but the undivided person, and therefore mortal (Gen. 2:7; 1 Cor. 15:45, "The first man Adam was made a living soul"; Ezek. 18:4, "the soul that sinneth, it shall die").
  • 1 Cor. 15:45. "And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit." — Paul quotes Genesis exactly: Adam WAS MADE a living soul, a created and dependent being, set over against the last Adam who gives life (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took").
  • CCh 74.4. White: "the human form was perfect in all its arrangements, but it was without life. Then a personal, self-existing God breathed into that form the breath of life.... Man became a living soul" — the formed body was lifeless until God breathed; the soul is what the whole man became, not what was inserted.
  • MH 415.1. White, in a parallel statement to CCh 74.4 above: "Man became a living soul. Through Christ the Word, a personal God created man and endowed him with intelligence and power." — the same paragraph read from another angle: intelligence itself is God's endowment upon the formed man, not the property of a pre-existing immortal spirit.

The breath defined — God's life-power, not a conscious tenant — Job 33:4; 27:3; Gen. 7:22; Ps. 104:29:

  • Job 33:4. "The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life." — Scripture defines its own figure: the breath is the Almighty's own life-giving power, the same act as creation, not a self-conscious entity lodged in the body.
    • the breath / spirit of life = the impersonal, God-given life-power that animates the dust — God's loaned inspiration, sustained heartbeat by heartbeat, never a self-aware being (Job 33:4; Job 27:3, "the spirit of God is in my nostrils"; Gen. 7:22; Ps. 104:29; Ps. 146:4).
  • Job 27:3. "All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils" — Job equates "my breath" with "the spirit of God": what animates man is the breath God breathed (Gen. 2:7), borrowed life-power, not man's own immortal core.
  • Gen. 7:22. "All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died." — the same breath of life is in beast and man alike, and when it departs they die; it is life-power common to all creatures, not a distinct conscious human essence.
  • Ps. 104:29. "thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust" — the exact inverse of Gen. 2:7: take away the breath and the creature dies; life is a loan sustained moment by moment.
  • 1SM 294.3. White: "Each heartbeat, each breath, is the inspiration of Him who breathed into the nostrils of Adam the breath of life—the inspiration of the ever-present God, the great I AM." — the breath is God's continually-renewed inspiration; man lives on borrowed life, never on a self-running immortal spark.

Death un-does Genesis 2:7 — dust to earth, breath to God — Gen. 3:19; Job 34:14-15; Eccl. 12:7; Ps. 146:4:

  • Gen. 3:19. "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" — God's own verdict on man's constitution and end: what was formed of dust dissolves back to dust; the created being is dissolved, not relocated.
  • Job 34:14-15. "If he ... gather unto himself his spirit and his breath; All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust." — the equation run in reverse: God gathers back His spirit and breath, and the WHOLE man perishes; withdraw the life-power and nothing conscious remains.
  • Eccl. 12:7. "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." — death resolves man into his two components: dust to earth, breath to Giver. The spirit "returns" exactly as it was given (Gen. 2:7) — as life-power reverting to its Source, not as the man flying to heaven.
  • Ps. 146:4. "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish." — the instant the breath departs, thoughts PERISH: consciousness ends with the breath; the returning spirit carries no mind with it — decisive against a thinking soul surviving death.
  • SBBS 314.10. Hales (Source Book): immortality is "not to be understood as being derived from any inherent virtue in his nature; as if the spirit or mind was necessarily immortal.... The divine sentence pronounced on Adam, 'Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return' (Genesis 3:19), included the dissolution of the spirit also." — nothing in man's nature is inherently immortal; "dust thou art" dissolves the whole man, spirit included.

The dead sleep — no knowledge, no praise, until the resurrection — Job 14:10-12; Eccl. 9:5; Ps. 6:5; 115:17:

  • Job 14:10. "But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?" — the question expects its answer: nowhere conscious; he is dissolved.
  • Job 14:12. "So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep." — death is a SLEEP, and its one exit is the resurrection; the sleeper waits for the waking, not for a flight.
  • Eccl. 9:5. "the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward" — no awareness, no reward yet; the undivided man is simply not conscious in death.
  • Ps. 6:5. "For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?" — no remembrance, no thanksgiving — no conscious activity of any kind.
  • Ps. 115:17. "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence." — the dead go down into silence, not up to conscious reward; death is stillness of the whole being, not the liberation of a praising soul.
  • DD 17.2. White: "The Bible clearly teaches that the dead do not go immediately to heaven. They are represented as sleeping until the resurrection.... man's thoughts perish." — Eccl. 9:5, Ps. 146:4, and Job 14 read together: no soul is awake in the intermediate state.

The soul is mortal — God only hath immortality, and the gift comes in Christ — Ezek. 18:4; 1 Tim. 6:16; 1 Cor. 15:22, 53; 2 Tim. 1:10:

  • Ezek. 18:4. "Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die." — Scripture's flat denial that the soul is deathless: since man IS a soul, the soul that sins is the whole man — and it dies. What that sin is, and how it attaches, is the next study (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance").
  • 1 Tim. 6:16. "Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto" — God ONLY hath immortality; man is mortal by nature and can receive immortality solely as a gift.
  • 1 Cor. 15:22. "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive." — all die in the mortal first man; life comes only in Christ, "made alive" at the resurrection.
  • 1 Cor. 15:53. "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." — man is "this mortal" NOW; immortality is a garment to be PUT ON at the resurrection, not a possession already carried.
  • 2 Tim. 1:10. "our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" — life and immortality come to light through Christ and the gospel: a gift brought by the Saviour, not native to fallen man.
  • GC 533.1. White: "Immortality, promised to man on condition of obedience, had been forfeited by transgression. Adam could not transmit to his posterity that which he did not possess... And only through Christ can immortality be obtained." — forfeited in Adam, obtainable only in Christ.
  • CET 39.4. White recalls the texts that settled her own mind: "'The soul that sinneth, it shall die.' Ezekiel 18:4. 'The living know that they shall die: but the dead know not anything.' Ecclesiastes 9:5. '...who only hath immortality.' 1 Timothy 6:15, 16." — the very spine of this section, cited together as proof the soul has no natural immortality.

The counter-doctrine — the serpent's first sermon — Gen. 3:4:

  • Gen. 3:4. "And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die." — the first lie denies God's verdict of Gen. 2:7 and 3:19: it teaches an undying something in man that death cannot touch; the immortal-soul theory is the serpent's sermon.
  • 1T 342.3. White: "The great original lie which he told to Eve in Eden, 'Ye shall not surely die,' was the first sermon ever preached on the immortality of the soul. That sermon was crowned with success, and terrible results followed." — the doctrine has a preacher, and it is the serpent.
  • DD 17.1. White: "The theory of the immortality of the soul was one of those false doctrines that Rome, borrowing from paganism, incorporated into the religion of Christendom. Martin Luther classed it with the 'monstrous fables that form part of the Roman dunghill of decretals.'" — the lie's road into Christendom runs through paganism and Rome, not through Scripture; the Reformer threw it out.

DEFINITION — DUST AND BREATH — WHAT MAN IS = man is dust of the ground made alive by the breath of God, and the sum is a LIVING SOUL (Gen. 2:7; 1 Cor. 15:45): he does not have a soul, he IS one — body, mind, and breath one indivisible being (CCh 74.4; MH 415.1). The breath/spirit is God's own loaned life-power (Job 33:4; 27:3), the same breath that animates the beasts (Gen. 7:22; Ps. 104:29), sustained heartbeat by heartbeat (1SM 294.3); it is not a conscious entity, for the day it goes forth "his thoughts perish" (Ps. 146:4). Death therefore un-does creation: dust to earth, spirit back to the God who gave it (Gen. 3:19; Eccl. 12:7; Job 34:14-15), dissolving the whole man, spirit included (SBBS 314.10), and the whole man sleeps in unconscious silence until the resurrection (Job 14:10-12; Eccl. 9:5; Ps. 6:5; 115:17; DD 17.2). The soul, then, is mortal — "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek. 18:4) — for God "only hath immortality" (1 Tim. 6:16), and mortal man must PUT ON immortality in Christ at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:22, 53; 2 Tim. 1:10; GC 533.1; CET 39.4). "Ye shall not surely die" (Gen. 3:4) — the immortal-soul theory — is the serpent's first sermon (1T 342.3), imported into Christendom from paganism through Rome and rejected by Luther (DD 17.1). This grounds the whole handbook: sin and salvation happen in ONE undivided man — body, mind, breath — not in an immortal ghost inside him; so sin is the whole man's own act (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance"), the whole man is the nature the Son of God took (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took"), and the whole man is what God saves from sin (see "What Salvation Really Is — Saved From Sin").

Symbols defined here:

  • the living soul = the whole man himself — the sum produced when God joined dust (body) to the breath of life; man does not have a soul, he IS one, an indivisible and mortal unit (Gen. 2:7; 1 Cor. 15:45; Ezek. 18:4; Eccl. 9:5; Ps. 146:4).
  • the breath / spirit of life = the impersonal, God-given life-power that animates the dust — common to man and beast, sustained moment by moment, returning to God at death as life-power without consciousness (Job 33:4; Job 27:3; Gen. 7:22; Ps. 104:29; Eccl. 12:7; Ps. 146:4; Job 34:14-15).

Symbols carried: none — this is the opening section; it establishes the WHOLE-MAN thread (dust + breath = a living soul, mortal and undivided) carried into "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance," "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took," and "What Salvation Really Is — Saved From Sin."

For discussion:

  1. Genesis 2:7 says man "became a living soul" — he does not receive one; and "each heartbeat, each breath" is the loaned inspiration of the God who breathed into Adam's nostrils (1SM 294.3). If the soul is what you ARE, and life is borrowed moment by moment, what changes this week in how you treat your body and mind — and what does daily dependence on Christ look like for a person who owns no life of his own (Gen. 2:7; 1 Tim. 6:16)?
  2. "The dead know not any thing" (Eccl. 9:5), and immortality is only "put on" at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:53). How does this make the resurrection — rather than death — the real center of the Christian hope, and how would you comfort a grieving friend from these texts?
  3. "His breath goeth forth... in that very day his thoughts perish" (Ps. 146:4). How does the truth that the dead sleep until the resurrection (Job 14:12) guard you against every deception — spiritualism, apparitions, voices claiming to be the dead — built on the serpent's "Ye shall not surely die" (Gen. 3:4)?

¶2. What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance

Sin is the transgression of the law — born only when the will consents, so guilt is by choice, never by birth; yet the fallen nature we do inherit is a real bondage, a bent that corrupts and enslaves the whole man until Christ delivers — corruption inherited: affirmed; guilt inherited: denied.

Sin is defined by the law, not by birth — 1 John 3:4:

  • 1 John 3:4. "Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law" — the Bible's own definition: sin IS the transgression of the law, a committed act against a known standard — "whosoever COMMITTETH" — not a condition of birth.
    • sin = the consented transgression of God's law — a chosen act against a known standard, born when desire conceives, when the will yields (1 John 3:4, "sin is the transgression of the law"; James 1:14-15, brought forth only "when lust hath conceived"; John 8:34, "Whosoever committeth sin"; Ezek. 18:20; Rom. 3:23, "all have sinned"). Defined by the law, never by lineage; guilt attaches to the choice, never to the mere presence of a fallen inclination.
  • AA 555.1. White: "'Whosoever committeth sin,' he writes, 'transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.'" — she lets John define sin, quoting the text verbatim and dealing "in plain terms" with sin as a DOING, an act against the law.

Sin has a genealogy — desire solicits, the will conceives — James 1:14-15; John 8:34:

  • James 1:14. "But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed" — the drawing and the enticing are temptation, not yet sin; the inward bent solicits.
  • James 1:15. "Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death" — sin has a birthday: it is BORN only when lust CONCEIVES — when the will says yes; the genealogy runs desire → consent → sin → death, and guilt enters at the consent.
  • John 8:34. "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" — Christ ties the bondage to the COMMITTING; the servitude of sin follows the act, not the ancestry — and the Son breaks that dominion (v. 36).
  • HP 251.3. White: "There is no sin in having temptation, but sin comes in when temptation is yielded to." — the precise James 1 distinction: the solicitation of the fallen nature is not sin; sin is born at the yielding of the will.
  • MYP 430.1. White: "It is Satan's act to tempt you, but your own act to yield. It is not in the power of all the host of Satan to force the tempted to transgress. There is no excuse for sin." — guilt is located at the personal act of yielding; no inherited or external force compels transgression.
  • 5T 177.1. White: "An impure thought tolerated, an unholy desire cherished, and the soul is contaminated... 'Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.'" — she traces sin's birth from a cherished, tolerated desire (the will's consent) to the act: conceived by the will, not by birth.
  • 2MCP 685.2. White: "This is the governing power in the nature of man—the power of decision, of choice. Everything depends on the right action of the will... Many will go down to ruin while hoping and desiring to overcome their evil propensities. They do not yield the will to God." — the will is the deciding power; guilt and ruin turn on its action, not on the mere existence of evil propensities.

Guilt is personal and non-transferable — Ezek. 18:4, 20; Deut. 24:16:

  • Ezek. 18:4. "Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die" — God claims every soul directly; each dies for its OWN sin, not the parent's (and the "soul" that dies is the whole man dying for his own sin, not a ghost punished for another's — see "Dust and Breath — What Man Is").
  • Ezek. 18:20. "The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son" — the flat rejection of inherited GUILT: no man is charged with another's iniquity, Adam's included.
  • Deut. 24:16. "The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin" — the judicial principle behind Ezekiel, written into the statute law of Israel: inherited guilt is foreign to God's government.
  • 1MR 142.3. White, preached at Minneapolis 1888 — the very session where Waggoner and Jones pressed righteousness by faith: "Well, you say, it was Adam's sin. You say, I am not guilty of that, and I am not responsible for his guilt and fall. Here all these natural tendencies are in me and I am not to blame if I act out these natural tendencies. Who is to blame? Is God?" — both sides held in one breath: not guilty of Adam's fall (inherited guilt denied), yet the natural tendencies really "in me" (corruption affirmed) — and blame attaches when we ACT them out.

Every mouth stopped — because all have sinned — Rom. 3:19, 23; 5:12:

  • Rom. 3:19. "that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God" — the law silences every defense; but the ground of the guilt is stated four verses on.
  • Rom. 3:23. "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" — the universal indictment rests on ACTS: "have sinned" is an active verb; every mouth is stopped because all have DONE, not because all were born.
  • Rom. 5:12. "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned" — death passed upon all, not because all inherited Adam's guilt, but "for that ALL HAVE SINNED": the universal reign of death traces to universal actual sinning, made possible by the fallen nature Adam introduced.

Yet the inherited corruption is real — shapen in iniquity — Ps. 51:5; Eph. 2:3:

  • Ps. 51:5. "Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me" — David is bent from birth: a fallen NATURE inherited, not a crime charged — a condition to be delivered from, not a guilt to be sentenced for.
    • the flesh / fallen nature = the inherited corruption — a real, terrible bent inclining toward evil, holding dominion over the natural man and enslaving him until Christ delivers; "sin that dwelleth in me" as a resident power, but NOT itself guilt — it condemns only when obeyed (Ps. 51:5, "shapen in iniquity"; Eph. 2:3, "by nature the children of wrath"; Rom. 7:14, "carnal, sold under sin"; Rom. 7:17-18, "sin that dwelleth in me... in my flesh"; Rom. 7:23, "a law in my members"; Rom. 7:24-25, delivered "through Jesus Christ"). Corruption inherited: affirmed. Guilt inherited: denied.
  • Eph. 2:3. "and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" — the fallen nature is real and universal; and mark where the wrath is bound in the same verse — to "fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind" — the nature condemns when OBEYED, not merely possessed.
  • CHR 26.2. Waggoner: "David had all the passions of human nature. He says of himself, 'Behold I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.' Psalm 51:5." — the inherited fallen nature established from Scripture: the flesh carries "all the weaknesses and sinful tendencies to which fallen human nature is subject," yet in the same argument no actual sin is conceded.
  • CHR 91.1. Waggoner: "We likewise can all say, with David, 'Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.' ... As a consequence, we are by nature so weak that we cannot do the things that we would." — Psalm 51:5 read as the confession of an inherited WEAKNESS that disables (echoing Rom. 7) — a bent to be delivered from by Christ's power, not a charged guilt.

A law in the members — the bent enslaves until Christ delivers — Rom. 7:14-25:

  • Rom. 7:14. "For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin" — the natural man is SOLD under sin: the fallen nature holds dominion — a slavery, not a mere guilt-tag.
  • Rom. 7:17-18. "it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me. For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing" — Paul distinguishes the indwelling sin in the flesh from the willing self: the nature is a resident power, corrupting but not identical with the person's guilt.
  • Rom. 7:23. "But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members" — the inherited bent operates as a LAW of the nature: it wars, it takes captive, it enslaves the natural man.
  • WOR 122.1. Waggoner, on Rom. 7:23: "I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind... This sin is in our flesh... But we are slaves. Whosoever commits sin is the slave of sin. John 8:34." — the law in the members is sin dwelling in the flesh, holding the natural man in bondage until liberty comes in Christ.
  • Rom. 7:24-25. "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord" — the nature is not a life sentence: deliverance comes "through Jesus Christ." Corruption is curable; guilt would not be.
  • CH 440.1. White: "Those who put their trust in Christ are not to be enslaved by any hereditary or cultivated habit or tendency... Whatever may be our inherited or cultivated tendencies to wrong, we can overcome through the power that He is ready to impart." — the hereditary tendency named as real bondage of the "lower nature," and named as OVERCOMABLE: precisely a bent, not a verdict.
  • LOF_ATJ 127.6. Jones: "that same degenerate, sinful flesh is there with its same tendencies and desires. But the individual is no longer subject to these... a power that conquers, brings under, crucifies, and keeps under, the flesh, sinful as it is, with all its affections and lusts." — the whole thesis in one line: the inherited flesh with its tendencies REMAINS even in the converted, yet the man is "no longer subject" to it — corruption real and enslaving, yet conquerable, not guilt (see "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame").

DEFINITION — WHAT SIN IS — TRANSGRESSION, NOT INHERITANCE = sin is the transgression of the law (1 John 3:4) — a consented act, born only "when lust hath conceived," when the will yields (James 1:14-15; HP 251.3; MYP 430.1); temptation is not sin, and no power in earth or hell can force the yielding (2MCP 685.2). Guilt is therefore personal and non-transferable: "the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" (Ezek. 18:4, 20; Deut. 24:16); every mouth is stopped and death reigns universal because "ALL HAVE SINNED" (Rom. 3:19, 23; 5:12), not because all were born — universal condemnation stands on universal sinning, not on inherited guilt. Yet what we DO inherit is real and terrible: a fallen nature, "shapen in iniquity" (Ps. 51:5), "by nature the children of wrath" (Eph. 2:3), "carnal, sold under sin" with "a law in my members" warring and taking captive (Rom. 7:14, 17-18, 23; WOR 122.1) — a corruption that inclines, enslaves, and holds dominion over the natural man, but is not itself guilt; it condemns only when obeyed (Eph. 2:3; 1MR 142.3; 2MCP 685.2), and it enslaves only until Christ delivers (Rom. 7:24-25; John 8:34, 36; LOF_ATJ 127.6; CH 440.1). Distinguish plainly and hold both: original-sin GUILT (guilty at birth) — rejected by the law and the prophets; inherited CORRUPTION (a bent that enslaves until Christ delivers) — affirmed by David and Paul alike, and curable where guilt would not be: "who shall deliver me?... I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Rom. 7:24-25). This distinction is the hinge of the handbook: it strips the sinner of every heredity-excuse ("there is no excuse for sin"), and it frees the doctrine of the incarnation — since guilt is not a substance bred in the flesh, the need it defines is not acquittal from Adam's crime but deliverance from sin's power (see "What Salvation Really Is — Saved From Sin"); because nature is not sin, Christ could take our fallen nature and be without sin (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took"); and because sin is in the consent, the consent can — by the same Christ — be forever withheld (see "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame").

Symbols defined here:

  • sin = the consented transgression of God's law — a chosen act against a known standard, born when desire conceives (the will yields); defined by the law, not by birth; guilt attaches to the choice, never to the mere presence of a fallen inclination (1 John 3:4; James 1:14-15; John 8:34; Ezek. 18:20; Rom. 3:23).
  • the flesh / fallen nature = the inherited corruption — a real bent that inclines toward evil and holds the natural man in bondage until Christ delivers; "sin that dwelleth in me" as a resident power, but not itself guilt — it condemns only when obeyed (Ps. 51:5; Eph. 2:3; Rom. 7:14, 17-18, 23-25).

Symbols carried: the living soul — the one whole man, dust + breath, who sins as one and dies as one, "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (see "Dust and Breath — What Man Is"); the fallen nature defined here is the very flesh the Son of God took, without its sin (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took"); the deliverance of Rom. 7:25 is entered by the new birth (see "Born of Water and of the Spirit — How He Lived, How We Begin") and carried to full dominion-breaking in the overcomer (see "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame").

For discussion:

  1. James 1:14-15 gives sin a birthday — "when lust hath conceived" — and White adds, "There is no sin in having temptation, but sin comes in when temptation is yielded to" (HP 251.3). In your own experience, where is the line between being tempted and consenting, and what does this distinction free a tempted believer from while leaving him responsible for?
  2. "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" (Ezek. 18:20). What excuse drawn from heredity, upbringing, or "that's just my nature" does this verse take away — "I am not to blame if I act out these natural tendencies. Who is to blame?" (1MR 142.3) — and what inherited tendency have you been treating as a verdict instead of a bondage Christ stands ready to break (CH 440.1)?
  3. Romans 7 ends not in despair but in thanksgiving (Rom. 7:24-25). For the bent you inherited, are you relying on resolve — "hoping and desiring to overcome" (2MCP 685.2) — or on the delivering power of Christ? How would the difference show in practice this week?

Part II — The Pattern

¶3. The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took

Two men stand at the head of the race: the first Adam fell in unfallen flesh; the second Adam conquered in ours — humanity as four thousand years of sin had left it, tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin — for the difference between Christ and us is not the flesh He bore but the life He lived in it.

Two Adams — two heads of the race — 1 Cor. 15:45-47; Rom. 5:19:

  • 1 Cor. 15:45. "The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit" — two representative men set over against each other; where the first head of the race fell, a second stands to reverse the ruin.
    • the second Adam = Christ as the new head and representative of the human race, standing where the first Adam fell — but in FALLEN flesh rather than unfallen, rendering unbroken obedience where the first man disobeyed: a real re-run of Adam's probation in the actual condition of Adam's ruined descendants, so that His obedience can be reckoned to the many just as Adam's disobedience was (1 Cor. 15:45, 47; Rom. 5:19, obedience against disobedience as the only contrast between the two heads; Heb. 2:16-17, the seed of Abraham, "made like unto his brethren" — His stand is inside fallen humanity, not above it).
  • 1 Cor. 15:46. "Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual" — the order is fixed: the natural man first, then the spiritual; the second Adam enters the natural man's arena to bring forth the spiritual.
  • 1 Cor. 15:47. "The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven" — the Lord from heaven enters the arena as "the second MAN": a real man of flesh, contesting the same field the first man lost.
  • Rom. 5:19. "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous" — the two heads are contrasted by obedience versus disobedience, not by two different natures; the whole weight of the figure falls on the LIFE each lived in the flesh he had.

Made of a woman, of the seed of David — the lineage He entered — Gal. 4:4-5; Rom. 1:3; Luke 1:35; John 1:14; Phil. 2:7-8:

  • Gal. 4:4. "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law" — He entered the human line through a fallen daughter of Adam, and took His stand under the law's curse where guilty man stood.
  • Gal. 4:5. "To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons" — the reason for the placement: only One standing where we stand can redeem us out of where we stand.
  • Rom. 1:3. "made of the seed of David according to the flesh" — not a body new-made as Adam's was in Eden, but David's actual lineage — David, who wrote "in sin did my mother conceive me" (Ps. 51:5); the flesh He took was that hereditary stream, four thousand years down from Eden.
  • CHR 26.2. Waggoner: "the flesh which He assumed had all the weaknesses and sinful tendencies to which fallen human nature is subject, is shown by the statement that He 'was made of the seed of David according to the flesh.' David had all the passions of human nature." — the pioneer reads Rom. 1:3 exactly so: David's seed, not a sinless being's, and Ps. 51:5 supplied as the receipt.
  • Luke 1:35. "that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God" — descended from a fallen woman, the hereditary line truly Mary's, yet the child is HOLY: the nature ours by descent, the character sinless from conception, both truths spoken by the angel in one breath (how that life was lived is walked in "Born of Water and of the Spirit — How He Lived, How We Begin").
  • John 1:14. "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" — MADE flesh, not clothed in the appearance of it; real, present, dwelling flesh, and in it the Father's glory beheld.
  • Phil. 2:7. "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men" — He emptied Himself all the way down into real, humbled humanity.
  • Phil. 2:8. "being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" — and in that humanity the triumph is one word: OBEDIENT — obedience unto death.

In the likeness of sinful flesh — real flesh, and sin condemned in it — Rom. 8:3-4:

  • Rom. 8:3. "God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh" — the law was "weak through the flesh," so God met sin on its own ground: the Son came in the likeness of SINFUL flesh — not the likeness of sinless flesh — and there, IN the flesh, condemned sin by never once yielding to it.
    • sinful flesh = the fallen, hereditary, degenerate human nature — weakened by four thousand years of sin, subject to infirmity and tempted from within and without — which Christ actually took ("likeness of sinful flesh" is real fallen flesh, not a mere appearance of it), and in which He never once consented to sin; it names the nature He bore, never any sin He committed, for nature is not sin and His consent never came (Rom. 8:3, sin condemned IN the flesh, not committed by Him; Rom. 1:3, the seed of David; Heb. 2:14, "took part of the same"; Heb. 4:15, "in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin"; 2 Cor. 5:21, "made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin").
  • WOR 126.6. Waggoner: "There is a common idea that this means that Christ simulated sinful flesh; that he did not take upon himself actual sinful flesh, but only what appeared to be such. But the Scriptures do not teach such a thing... He took the same flesh that all have who are born of woman." — the phantom-flesh escape hatch closed; "likeness" is not pretence.
  • Rom. 8:4. "That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit" — the purpose of v. 3: because sin was met and mastered in the very flesh we wear, the law's righteousness can now be fulfilled IN US; His victory in fallen flesh is the pledge of ours.
  • WOR 127.2. Waggoner: "Even so Christ came in the same sinful flesh, yet he was without sin, because he was always led by the Spirit." — both truths in one sentence, and the reason named: the LIFE ("always led by the Spirit"), not a different nature.

The same flesh and blood — in all things like unto His brethren — Heb. 2:14-18:

  • Heb. 2:14. "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same" — THE SAME: the same flesh and blood the children have, taken "that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil."
  • Heb. 2:15. "And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage" — He entered the bondage to break it from inside.
  • Heb. 2:16. "For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham" — not an unfallen angel-nature; a son of Abraham's fallen line.
  • Heb. 2:17. "Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest" — IN ALL THINGS: "the same" and "in all things" bar every escape hatch that would hand Him a different, unfallen humanity.
  • Heb. 2:18. "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted" — the temptation was real SUFFERING, not a staged demonstration; only one tempted in our flesh can succour the tempted.
  • CWCP 27.1-2. Jones: "He was made in the likeness of men, as men are, just where they are. 'The Word was made flesh.' He 'took part of the same' flesh and blood as that of which the children of men are partakers, as they are since man has fallen into sin." — Phil. 2, John 1:14, Heb. 2:14, and Gal. 4:4 walked as one thread: the flesh as it is SINCE the fall.
  • 3SM 197.3. White: "But many say that Jesus was not like us... But Paul writes, 'Verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham. Wherefore in all things it behooved him to be made like unto his brethren...'" — she answers the very objection this section confronts by driving straight to Heb. 2:16-17.

Humanity at its weakest — four thousand years down from Eden — Isa. 53:2-3:

  • Isa. 53:2. "he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness" — prophecy fixed the condition beforehand: a root out of DRY ground, humanity with no advantage of soil and no reserves.
  • Isa. 53:3. "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief... he was despised, and we esteemed him not" — He wore humanity at its weakest and most unlovely; degenerate flesh, not glorified Adam-flesh.
  • DA 48.6. White: "It would have been an almost infinite humiliation for the Son of God to take man's nature, even when Adam stood in his innocence in Eden. But Jesus accepted humanity when the race had been weakened by four thousand years of sin. Like every child of Adam He accepted the results of the working of the great law of heredity." — the pre-fall theory settled: not Eden's flesh, but the line as heredity had left it.
  • DA 117.1-2. White: "Christ took upon Him the infirmities of degenerate humanity... He took the nature of man, with the possibility of yielding to temptation." — degenerate humanity, all its liabilities, a real possibility of failure — or He could not have been placed in Adam's position at all.

Tempted in all points — yet without sin — the double guard — Heb. 4:15; 2 Cor. 5:21; 1 Pet. 2:22:

  • Heb. 4:15. "we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin" — both guards in one verse: IN ALL POINTS TEMPTED LIKE AS WE ARE (full identity of nature and temptation), YET WITHOUT SIN (absolute sinlessness). Hold both with equal force; drop either and the High Priest is lost.
  • 2 Cor. 5:21. "he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin" — the strongest pairing in Scripture: MADE to be sin (the full weight of fallen flesh and the sinner's condemnation laid on Him) — who KNEW NO SIN (consent never came). Nature and character held apart in six words.
  • 1 Pet. 2:22. "Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" — in the fallen flesh He bore, the record is spotless: not once.
  • 1SM 253.1. White: "Christ, who knew not the least taint of sin or defilement, took our nature in its deteriorated condition." — both truths in one line: the deteriorated nature ours, the defilement never His.
  • 1SM 256.1. White: "In taking upon Himself man's nature in its fallen condition, Christ did not in the least participate in its sin... He was touched with the feeling of our infirmities, and was in all points tempted like as we are. And yet He knew no sin." — from the chapter titled "Sinlessness of Christ's Human Nature": fallen nature, zero participation in its sin.
  • FLB 49.4. White: "He could have sinned; He could have fallen, but not for one moment was there in Him an evil propensity." — quoted honestly: the risk was real ("He could have fallen") and the sinlessness total; the guard is about consent and character — no evil cherished — not a retraction of the fallen nature He took, for nature is not sin (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance").

The difference is the life, not the flesh — Heb. 5:8-9:

  • Heb. 5:8. "Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered" — a real moral warfare, really fought: obedience LEARNED in suffering, not exempted from it.
  • Heb. 5:9. "And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him" — perfected through that warfare, He is author of salvation to all who by the same surrender obey.
  • CWCP 84.1. Jones: "Christ attained it in human flesh in this world and thus made and consecrated a way by which, in Him, every believer can attain it." — perfection of character attained IN human flesh opens the same road to the believer (walked out in "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame").
  • DA 664.4. White: "Jesus revealed no qualities, and exercised no powers, that men may not have through faith in Him. His perfect humanity is that which all His followers may possess, if they will be in subjection to God as He was." — the closing conviction: the difference is the life lived, and that life is offered to us.
  • LOF_ATJ 60.2. Jones: "There is a mystery in how God can be manifest in such sinful flesh as yours." — the doctrine pressed home personally: the flesh He took is YOUR flesh, and that is the ground of your hope.

DEFINITION — THE SECOND ADAM — THE NATURE CHRIST TOOK = Christ is the last Adam, the second man (1 Cor. 15:45-47), the new head of the race whose obedience is set against the first man's disobedience (Rom. 5:19) — and He re-ran Adam's probation NOT in Adam's unfallen Eden flesh but in the actual condition of Adam's ruined descendants. He was made of a woman, made under the law (Gal. 4:4-5), of the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3; cf. Ps. 51:5), made flesh indeed (John 1:14; Phil. 2:7-8), in the likeness of sinful flesh — real fallen flesh, not a simulation (Rom. 8:3; WOR 126.6) — the same flesh and blood as the children, the seed of Abraham, made like unto His brethren in all things (Heb. 2:14-17): humanity as four thousand years of heredity had left it, degenerate, with all its liabilities (Isa. 53:2-3; DA 48.6; DA 117.1-2). In that flesh He was in all points tempted like as we are, YET WITHOUT SIN (Heb. 4:15); made to be sin, yet He knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21); He did no sin (1 Pet. 2:22); that which was born is "that holy thing" (Luke 1:35) — for "sinful flesh" names the nature He bore, never any sin He committed: nature is not sin, and consent never came (1SM 253.1; 1SM 256.1; FLB 49.4). The difference between Christ and us is therefore not the flesh He wore but the life He lived in it — obedience learned through suffering, "always led by the Spirit" (Heb. 5:8-9; WOR 127.2) — and the purpose of the whole arrangement is Rom. 8:4: sin condemned in the flesh "that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us." This is the ground Waggoner (CHR, 1890) and Jones (CWCP, 1905) developed from the 1888 Minneapolis message on righteousness by faith, and that Ellen White guarded through the same 1890s controversy (1SM 253-256; FLB 49.4; 3SM 197.3): a Saviour near enough to be tempted as we are, sinless enough to save, whose victory in our flesh is the pledge and pattern of ours.

Symbols defined here:

  • the second Adam = Christ as the new head and representative of the human race, standing where the first Adam fell — in fallen flesh, rendering unbroken obedience where the first man disobeyed, a real re-run of Adam's probation in the condition of Adam's ruined descendants, His obedience reckoned to the many as Adam's disobedience was (1 Cor. 15:45, 47; Rom. 5:19; Heb. 2:16-17).
  • sinful flesh = the fallen, hereditary, degenerate human nature — weakened by four thousand years of sin, tempted from within and without — which Christ actually took and in which He never once consented to sin; the nature He bore, never any sin He committed (Rom. 8:3; Rom. 1:3; Heb. 2:14; Heb. 4:15; 2 Cor. 5:21).

Symbols carried: the living soul — the first Adam "was made a living soul" (1 Cor. 15:45), the whole undivided man the second Adam took (defined in "Dust and Breath — What Man Is"); sin as consented transgression, and the fallen nature that is not itself guilt — the distinction that lets Christ take our flesh without our sin (defined in "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance"). Carried forward: the Spirit-led life by which He overcame in this flesh is walked in "Born of Water and of the Spirit — How He Lived, How We Begin", and His victory in fallen flesh as the pledge of ours is taken up in "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame".

For discussion:

  1. Heb. 2:17 says "in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren." If Christ had taken Adam's unfallen nature instead of ours, what becomes of Heb. 2:18 — could He still "succour them that are tempted," and could you still bring Him your actual temptations?
  2. Rom. 8:3 ends in Rom. 8:4: sin was condemned in the flesh "that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us." What does Christ's obedience in your flesh — not in a better flesh — mean for the sin you have privately called unconquerable?
  3. He "himself hath suffered being tempted" and is therefore "able to succour them that are tempted" (Heb. 2:18). When temptation comes this week, what changes in your praying if the High Priest you approach has felt the full pull of your flesh — and never once consented?

¶4. Born of Water and of the Spirit — How He Lived, How We Begin

Christ began human life conceived of the Holy Ghost and lived it in unbroken dependence on the indwelling Father — and what He was from His first birth, we become by the second: born of water and of the Spirit, cleansing joined to power, a new creature partaking of the divine nature.

Conceived of the Holy Ghost — the life begins in the Spirit — Matt. 1:20; Luke 1:35:

  • Matt. 1:20. "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" — His human life begins IN the Spirit; before a word is spoken or a work done, the Son enters our flesh already inside the Spirit-filled, God-surrendered existence — He never knew any other.
  • Luke 1:35. "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God" — mark the two agents of His birth: the Holy Ghost, and the power of the Highest; this exact vocabulary returns upon the church (Acts 1:8).
  • 1SM 226.2. White: "In His humanity He was a partaker of the divine nature. In His incarnation He gained in a new sense the title of the Son of God" — in OUR nature (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took") He was Himself "a partaker of the divine nature" — the very phrase afterward written over the believer (2 Pet. 1:4).
  • MWM 302.1. Millerite conference report (Memoirs of William Miller): the first advent "took place in the days of Herod, when He was conceived of the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary" — a settled first-advent fact: the Spirit-filled life this section traces starts at His conception.

From childhood the Father's will was His life — Luke 2:49; Ps. 40:8:

  • Luke 2:49. "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" — twelve years old, and the Father's will is already the "must" of His existence; the surrendered life did not begin at Jordan — it was His from the first.
  • Ps. 40:8. "I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart" — the Messianic key: the law WITHIN the heart, obedience by delight and not constraint — the very thing the new birth writes in us (Eze. 36:26-27).

How He lived — the Son can do nothing of Himself — John 5:19, 30; 14:10; Heb. 5:8-9; John 6:57; Gal. 2:20:

  • John 5:19. "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do" — the astonishing disclaimer: in the flesh He took, Christ renounces independent power; He lived as man must live — by dependence.
  • John 5:30. "I can of mine own self do nothing... I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me" — the confession restated: not His own will but the Father's; the surrendered will is the mechanism of the sinless life.
  • John 14:10. "the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works" — the works were the Father's, wrought through an indwelt, surrendered man — the very arrangement offered to us.
  • DA 208.2. White: "So utterly was Christ emptied of self that He made no plans for Himself. He accepted God's plans for Him... So should we depend upon God, that our lives may be the simple outworking of His will" — His "can do nothing of Himself" means total surrender and total dependence — and the sentence ends on us: "so should we."
  • SC 75.2. White: "The Saviour has said of Himself, 'The Son can do nothing of Himself;' 'the Father that dwelleth in Me, He doeth the works.'... We shall work as He worked; we shall manifest the same spirit" — John 5:19 and 14:10 read as one truth and handed straight to the believer.
  • DA 363.1. White: "As a man He supplicated the throne of God till His humanity was charged with a heavenly current that should connect humanity with divinity... His experience is to be ours" — the channel named: AS A MAN He drew from God; power came by dependence, prayed for and received — and the paragraph closes by handing that experience over.
  • Heb. 5:8-9. "Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered; and being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him" — obedience LEARNED, in suffering flesh: the sinless life was a lived acquisition, not an exercised advantage — and its fruit is salvation "unto all them that obey him."
  • CHR 27.3. Waggoner: "not only counted as a sinner but actually taking upon Himself sinful nature... 'in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin'" — the nature was ours (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took"); the sinlessness was in never consenting — for sin is in the consent, not the flesh (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance").
  • DA 117.2. White: "our Saviour took humanity, with all its liabilities. He took the nature of man, with the possibility of yielding to temptation. We have nothing to bear which He has not endured" — therefore His victory was won by no advantage withheld from us; what He used, we may use.
  • John 6:57. "As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me" — Christ names His own life-principle and hands it over in the same breath: the dependence He lived by becomes the dependence we live by.
  • Gal. 2:20. "the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God" — the mechanism made explicit: the indwelt, surrendered life is lived BY FAITH — and not a faith we manufacture, but "the faith of the Son of God," His own faith imparted.

What He was by birth, we become by the new birth — John 3:3-7:

  • John 3:3. "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" — not reform, not resolve: a BIRTH; nothing less can even see the kingdom.
  • John 3:4. "How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?" — Nicodemus's bewilderment measures the demand: the change required is as total as beginning life over.
  • John 3:5. "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God" — the charter of the second birth: water AND Spirit, together, or no entrance.
    • the new birth (born again / born of water and of the Spirit) = the Spirit re-creating the whole man — "an entire change of the entire man" (TDG 48.4), a new heart and new spirit given (Eze. 36:26-27), making a "new creature" (2 Cor. 5:17) able to see and enter the kingdom — the second birth that puts a man where Christ stood from His first: inside the Spirit-filled, God-surrendered life (John 3:5-7; Titus 3:5; 2 Pet. 1:4).
  • John 3:6. "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" — the flesh reproduces only itself (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance"); only a second parentage produces a second kind of man.
  • John 3:7. "Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again" — His "must" was the Father's business (Luke 2:49); ours is the birth that brings us into it.
  • DA 171.5. White: "Nicodemus knew that Christ here referred to water baptism and the renewing of the heart by the Spirit of God" — water = baptism; Spirit = the renewed heart; the two are one requirement, not two.
  • TDG 48.4. White: "Transformation of heart means an entire change of the entire man... it is an inward work, and yet, it is seen, because it works outward from within" — the new birth is total, and it shows.

The washing — the laver of regeneration — cleansing joined to power — Titus 3:5; Eph. 5:26; Eze. 36:25-27:

  • Titus 3:5. "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost" — the two clauses are one act: washing (cleansing) joined to renewing (power), and neither is by works.
    • the washing / the laver of regeneration (regeneration by water, word, and Spirit) = the cleansing of regeneration in which washing and power are inseparable — the clean water (Eze. 36:25), the word (Eph. 5:26), and the renewing Spirit (Titus 3:5) are one act, which both removes the filthiness AND puts the Spirit within to cause the cleansed one to walk in God's statutes (Eze. 36:27; Zech. 4:6).
  • Eph. 5:26. "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word" — the washing water is the word: the cleansing is wrought by water and word and Spirit together (John 3:5; Titus 3:5).
  • Eze. 36:25. "Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you" — the OT washing-promise: God does the sprinkling and God does the cleansing.
  • Eze. 36:26. "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh" — the washing is joined to a transplant: stony heart out, heart of flesh in — the new birth in prophecy.
  • Eze. 36:27. "And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them" — cleansing (v. 25) is joined to power (v. 27): the indwelling Spirit CAUSES the walk — the delight-obedience Christ had from birth (Ps. 40:8) now promised to us.
  • SD 105.3. White: "All true reformation begins with soul-cleansing. It is by the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the mind through the power of the Holy Spirit, that a change is wrought in the life" — washing and power never separated; a cleansing without the Spirit's renewing is no regeneration.

Not by might — the power named and offered — Zech. 4:6; Acts 1:8:

  • Zech. 4:6. "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts" — the power-source of the whole re-creation named once for all: human might is expressly ruled out — the Spirit-not-flesh principle by which Christ lived and by which we are re-made.
  • COL 66.1. White: "As the plant receives the sunshine, the dew, and the rain, we are to open our hearts to the Holy Spirit. The work is to be done 'not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit, saith the Lord of hosts'" — after the birth, growth runs by the same law: receiving, not achieving.
  • Acts 1:8. "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me" — hear Luke 1:35 again: the Holy Ghost "come upon," the power of the Highest — the overshadowing of His birth becomes the endowment of ours.

The result — a new creature, partaker of the divine nature — 2 Cor. 5:17; 2 Pet. 1:4:

  • 2 Cor. 5:17. "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new" — the finished result: not the old man improved but a new creation, living from the same source Christ lived from.
  • 2 Pet. 1:4. "that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust" — the very phrase 1SM 226.2 used of Christ's humanity is now written over the believer: what He was, we are made.
  • CWCP 43.4. Jones: "God sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh... condemned sin in the flesh: that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit... for to make in Himself of twain [God and man] one new man" — the purpose of the incarnation lands here: righteousness fulfilled IN US who walk after the Spirit; the "one new man" is the new creature of 2 Cor. 5:17 — the ground of "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame."

DEFINITION — BORN OF WATER AND OF THE SPIRIT — HOW HE LIVED, HOW WE BEGIN = Christ's human life began in the Spirit — conceived of the Holy Ghost (Matt. 1:20; MWM 302.1), "that holy thing" made by the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest (Luke 1:35), Himself in His humanity "a partaker of the divine nature" (1SM 226.2) — and it was lived the whole way in surrendered dependence: the Father's business from childhood (Luke 2:49), the law within the heart (Ps. 40:8), "the Son can do nothing of himself" (John 5:19, 30), "the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works" (John 14:10; DA 208.2; SC 75.2; DA 363.1), obedience learned in suffering flesh (Heb. 5:8-9). He overcame by no power unavailable to us (DA 117.2; CHR 27.3), and He hands the arrangement over intact: "I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me" (John 6:57) — a life lived thereafter "by the faith of the Son of God" (Gal. 2:20). What He was from His first birth we become by the second: born of water and of the Spirit (John 3:3-7) — the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost (Titus 3:5), the washing of water by the word (Eph. 5:26), the sprinkled clean water, the given heart, and the indwelling Spirit that causes the walk (Eze. 36:25-27) — an entire change of the entire man (TDG 48.4), cleansing joined to power, not by might nor by power but by His Spirit (Zech. 4:6), the Holy Ghost coming upon us as upon Mary (Luke 1:35 → Acts 1:8). The result is a new creature (2 Cor. 5:17), a partaker of the divine nature (2 Pet. 1:4; CWCP 43.4) — a man begun where Christ began, living from the source Christ lived from, so that overcoming as He overcame (see "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame") is not imitation from without but the outworking of the same indwelt life.

Symbols defined here:

  • the new birth (born again / born of water and of the Spirit) = the Spirit re-creating the whole man — an entire change of the entire man, a new heart and new spirit given, so that the man becomes a new creature able to see and enter the kingdom; the second birth that puts a man where Christ stood from His first birth, inside the Spirit-filled, God-surrendered life (John 3:3-7; 2 Cor. 5:17; Eze. 36:26-27; Titus 3:5; 2 Pet. 1:4; TDG 48.4).
  • the washing / the laver of regeneration (regeneration by water, word, and Spirit) = the cleansing of regeneration in which washing and power are joined and inseparable — water sprinkled clean, the word that sanctifies, and the renewing of the Holy Ghost are one act, removing filthiness AND supplying the indwelling Spirit that causes the cleansed one to walk in God's statutes; not by might or works, but by the Spirit (Titus 3:5; Eph. 5:26; Eze. 36:25-27; Zech. 4:6; SD 105.3).

Symbols carried: the second Adam and sinful flesh — the nature He lived this life in (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took"); sin as consented transgression and the flesh / fallen nature that reproduces only itself (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance"); the living soul — the new birth re-creates the WHOLE man because man is one undivided whole (see "Dust and Breath — What Man Is").

For discussion:

  1. Christ said, "The Son can do nothing of himself" (John 5:19) and "I live by the Father" (John 6:57). Where in this week's decisions are you still living "of your own self" — and what would it look like, concretely, to live those hours by dependence as He did?
  2. Ezekiel 36:25-27 joins the cleansing to the Spirit who "causes" obedience, and Titus 3:5 joins the washing to the renewing. Which half have you been attempting alone — cleansing without power, or power without cleansing — and what does receiving both as ONE act change about how you pray?
  3. Jesus was born into the Spirit-filled life; we must be born into it (John 3:7). If Acts 1:8 is the believer's birthright and not merely the apostles' history, what would you begin asking God for differently tomorrow morning?

Part III — The Remedy

¶5. What Salvation Really Is — Saved From Sin

The angel named the Saviour by His work — "he shall save his people FROM their sins" — from sin's guilt, from sin's dominion, and at last from sin's very presence, by the indwelling Christ restoring the image of God in the soul; a gospel that leaves men under sin's rule until death is not the everlasting gospel.

The Saviour is named by His work — Matt. 1:21, 23; Ps. 130:8:

  • Matt. 1:21. "thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins" — the name is the work: He saves His people FROM their sins — not from the penalty only, and never leaving them IN them; Jesus (Heb. Yeshua) = "Jehovah saves," and what Jehovah saves from is the sin itself.
    • salvation = God saving man FROM sin — from its guilt (justification, the pardon of Matt. 1:21), from its power and dominion (sanctification, Rom. 6:14, 18, 22; John 8:36), and at last from its very presence (glorification, 1 John 3:2); the restoration of the image of God in the soul (Col. 3:10; 2 Cor. 3:18), effected by the indwelling Christ (Col. 1:27; Gal. 2:20), reaching "to the uttermost" (Heb. 7:25) — not a legal status only but a Person possessed and a nature renewed.
  • Matt. 1:23. "they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us" — the paired name gives the method: He saves from sin by being God WITH us — and, the mystery carried to its end, God IN us (Col. 1:27); the Person present is the power that saves.
  • Ps. 130:8. "And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities" — the Old Testament promise Matthew 1:21 fulfils: redemption FROM all iniquities, not toleration of them; "all" leaves no reserved sin under which the redeemed remain.
  • EVCO 18.1. Waggoner: "It is a message of salvation from sin" — the everlasting gospel named in one sentence, grounded on the angel's word to Joseph in Matthew 1:21.

What sin is, He treats as bondage — and breaks it — John 8:34-36:

  • John 8:34. "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" — Christ's diagnosis: sin is not a debt only but a slavery; the consented transgression (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance") makes the sinner a slave.
  • John 8:35. "the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the Son abideth ever" — the slave has no standing in the house; only the Son can confer a sonship that abides.
  • John 8:36. "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" — the freedom He gives is not nominal; "indeed" — it actually severs the slavery.
  • DA 466.3. White: "Christ came to break the shackles of sin-slavery from the soul" — quoting John 8:36 itself; the soul that refuses to give himself to God "may talk of freedom, but he is in the most abject slavery" — the pardon that leaves the chains on is not the freedom Christ gives.

Made free from sin — guilt and dominion dealt with together — Rom. 6:6, 14, 18, 22:

  • Rom. 6:6. our old man is crucified with Him, "that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin" — the cross's stated purpose in the believer: not forgiven continuance in sin, but the end of sin's service.
  • Rom. 6:14. "For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace" — this is grace's own definition: deliverance from sin's DOMINION; a gospel that leaves men under sin's rule contradicts the very clause that defines being "under grace" (walked in full in "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame").
  • Rom. 6:18. "Being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness" — the section's term verbatim, in the present tense: freedom from sin is a stated fact for the believer, issuing at once in a new servitude — to righteousness.
  • Rom. 6:22. "But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life" — the whole arc in one verse: freedom now, holiness as fruit, everlasting life at the end.
  • WOR 71.1. Waggoner: the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness is "the blessedness of sins forgiven, and of freedom from the power of sin" — pardon and power are one blessedness, never separated in the gospel.
  • LOF_ATJ 147.4. Jones, on Rom. 6:18: "Being then made free from sin, YE BECAME THE SERVANTS OF RIGHTEOUSNESS.... He says you are, and when He says you are, it is so.... He has made you so, for He says so" — the deliverance is received on God's word, as fact.
  • LOF_ATJ 85.2. Jones: the power of God is given for "deliverance from sin and from the power of it, the reign of righteousness in the life" — and he rebukes the truncated gospel: "Many believe and receive the grace of God for the salvation from sins that are past but are content with that and do not give it the same place in the soul to reign against the power of sin."
  • GTI 190.2. Waggoner: coming to Jesus, the Mediator of the new covenant, "we become free from sin,—from transgression of the law" — with "grace to help us in the hour of temptation" and "cleansing from all sin"; the freedom reaches the very hour of the trial.

The righteousness of the law fulfilled IN us — God works the obedience — Rom. 8:3-4; Eze. 36:25-27:

  • Rom. 8:3. "God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh" — in the very flesh He took (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took"), sin was condemned — dethroned in its own stronghold.
  • Rom. 8:4. "That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit" — the purpose clause of the incarnation: not imputed righteousness only, but the law's righteousness wrought IN the believer by the Spirit.
  • GTI 199.1. Waggoner: "And why does He make us free from sin?—In order that we may live free from sin" — Christ, who has power over all flesh, strengthens us by His Spirit "that the righteousness of the law may be fulfilled in us."
  • Eze. 36:25. "Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you" — the covenant promise beneath the whole New Testament: cleansing from ALL filthiness, defilement removed, not managed.
  • Eze. 36:26-27. "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you... I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" — God Himself works the walking; salvation from sin's power is a divine operation, not a human resolve — the new-birth promise in covenant form (see "Born of Water and of the Spirit — How He Lived, How We Begin").

The power of it is not a status but a Person — Col. 1:27; Gal. 2:20:

  • Col. 1:27. "which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" — the mystery of the gospel is not a ledger entry only but a Person possessed; the indwelling Saviour is Himself the pledge that the work will be finished.
  • Gal. 2:20. "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God" — the mechanism of salvation from sin's power: the old self crucified, and an indwelling Life living the new life "in the flesh" by faith — not the man's effort, but Christ's own living.
  • CT 194.1. White: "When Christ is formed within, the hope of glory, then the truth of God will so act upon the natural temperament that its transforming power will be seen in changed characters" — the authority of God over the man "not in name only, but in reality and truth."
  • EVCO 23.2. Waggoner: "the power by which Christ saves men from sin is the power by which He created the worlds" — the everlasting gospel preaches Christ "the creative power of God"; salvation from sin is a Creator's act, a re-creation, not a reform.

What is being restored: the image of God — Col. 3:9-10; 2 Cor. 3:18:

  • Col. 3:9. "seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds" — the old man is put OFF, deeds and all; salvation does not whitewash him, it removes him.
  • Col. 3:10. "put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him" — the new man is renewed after the Creator's own image: salvation reverses the fall by re-creating in the soul the likeness that sin marred.
  • 2 Cor. 3:18. "beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory" — the process named: progressive transformation into Christ's image by beholding Him, wrought "as by the Spirit of the Lord" — Colossians 3:10 in motion.
  • DA 37.3. White: "Jesus came to restore in man the image of his Maker. None but Christ can fashion anew the character that has been ruined by sin" — He came "to reshape the marred character after the pattern of His divine character."
  • Ed 125.2. White: the central theme of the whole Bible is "the redemption plan, the restoration in the human soul of the image of God" — salvation from sin IS image-restoration; the two are one definition.

To the uttermost — sins taken away, the devil's works destroyed — Heb. 7:25; 1 John 3:5, 8; Titus 2:14:

  • Heb. 7:25. "he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them" — the section's term verbatim: to the UTTERMOST — completely, to the last extremity of sin's hold; His unbroken priestly life guarantees a salvation that reaches all the way, not a partial rescue.
  • 1 John 3:5. "he was manifested to take away our sins; and in him is no sin" — removal, not mere covering; the sinless One was manifested for the express purpose of taking sin AWAY.
  • 1 John 3:8. "For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil" — sin is the devil's work; a salvation that leaves that work intact in the saved fails the very purpose for which the Son was manifested.
  • Titus 2:14. "that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works" — Christ's self-gift has twin objects: redemption from all iniquity and purification of a people; guilt and defilement dealt with together.
  • PCP 48.2. White: "He takes away our sins, and makes us partakers of His holiness.... He is able to save unto the uttermost all who come unto God by Him" — removal of sin joined to impartation of holiness; the two halves of the uttermost salvation.

And at last, from sin's presence — a people without spot — 1 John 3:2-3; Eph. 5:25-27:

  • 1 John 3:2. "now are we the sons of God... when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" — glorification: the last stage of salvation, deliverance from sin's very PRESENCE at His appearing.
  • 1 John 3:3. "And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure" — the future likeness works backward: the hope of being like Him purifies NOW, "even as he is pure."
  • Eph. 5:25-26. "Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word" — the present tense of His love: sanctifying and cleansing now.
  • Eph. 5:27. "That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" — the end of the everlasting gospel: a people actually cleansed from sin, not merely accounted so — the church He presents at last (ripened in "The Harvest — A People in Whom Christ Is Vindicated").

DEFINITION — WHAT SALVATION REALLY IS — SAVED FROM SIN = salvation is God saving His people FROM their sins (Matt. 1:21; Ps. 130:8) — from sin's guilt in justification, the pardon of Matt. 1:21 ("the blessedness of sins forgiven," WOR 71.1), from sin's power and dominion in sanctification ("being then made free from sin," Rom. 6:14, 18, 22; "free indeed," John 8:36), and at last from sin's very presence in glorification ("we shall be like him," 1 John 3:2; "not having spot, or wrinkle," Eph. 5:27). It is the restoration of the image of God in the soul (Col. 3:9-10; 2 Cor. 3:18; DA 37.3; Ed 125.2), and its power is not a legal status only but a Person possessed — "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Col. 1:27), the crucified-with-Christ life in which "Christ liveth in me" (Gal. 2:20) — the same creative power that made the worlds (EVCO 23.2) now working in the believer what God promised in the covenant: "I will... cause you to walk in my statutes" (Eze. 36:25-27; Rom. 8:3-4). Christ was manifested "to take away our sins" and "destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:5, 8), and He "is able also to save them to the uttermost" (Heb. 7:25) — therefore, as the message that came to the fore at Minneapolis in 1888 and was preached in the years following pressed home (LOF_ATJ 85.2; GTI 199.1), a gospel that receives grace only for "sins that are past" while leaving sin's power enthroned, a gospel that leaves men under sin's dominion until death, is not the everlasting gospel; it is salvation IN sin, and the angel's word forbids it: He saves His people FROM their sins.

Symbols defined here:

  • salvation = God saving man FROM sin — from its guilt (justification), from its power and dominion (sanctification), and at last from its very presence (glorification); the restoration of the image of God in the soul by the indwelling Christ — not a legal status only but a Person possessed and a nature renewed — reaching to the uttermost (Matt. 1:21; Ps. 130:8; Rom. 6:18, 22; John 8:36; Col. 3:10; 2 Cor. 3:18; Col. 1:27; Gal. 2:20; Heb. 7:25; 1 John 3:2-3, 5, 8; Titus 2:14).

Symbols carried: sin = the consented transgression of the law, the slavery here broken (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance"); the likeness of sinful flesh in which sin was condemned = the nature Christ took (see "The Second Adam — The Nature Christ Took"); the new heart and the washing = the new birth by water and the Spirit (see "Born of Water and of the Spirit — How He Lived, How We Begin"); the faith by which Christ lives in the believer is walked in full in "Righteousness by Faith — The Third Angel’s Message in Verity," and the dominion broken here is proved complete in "Complete Victory — Overcoming as He Overcame."

For discussion:

  1. Matt. 1:21 says He saves His people "from their sins," and Jones warns of those who "receive the grace of God for the salvation from sins that are past but are content with that." Where in your own life have you quietly settled for pardon without deliverance — and what would it mean this week to claim Rom. 6:14 as a promise rather than an ideal?
  2. Rom. 6:14 makes freedom from sin's dominion the very definition of being "under grace." Is there a "reserved sin" you have quietly accepted as permanent — and what does "I will... cause you to walk in my statutes" (Eze. 36:27) promise about that very thing?
  3. Col. 1:27 and Gal. 2:20 make salvation a Person possessed, not a status only. In the next real temptation, what is the practical difference between trusting a changed record in heaven and trusting Christ living in you at that moment?

¶6. Righteousness by Faith — The Third Angel’s Message in Verity

The remedy for sin is a righteousness not our own — its very name is THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS: Christ's obedience COUNTED to the believer for his title, and Christ Himself LIVING in the believer for his fitness — one gift, received and lived by faith alone; and this, said the messenger of the Lord, is the third angel's message in verity.

The righteousness of God, without the law, upon all them that believe — Rom. 3:21-28; 5:1:

  • Rom. 3:21. "But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets" — the remedy is not a better law-keeping manufactured by man but a righteousness GOD supplies; the law and the prophets witnessed to it all along.
    • righteousness by faith = Christ's own righteousness given to the believer in two inseparable modes: IMPUTED — His obedience counted to the one who believes, the TITLE (Rom. 3:24-28; Rom. 4:3-5); and IMPARTED — the same Christ living in the believer by faith, the FITNESS (Gal. 2:20; Rom. 8:3-4; 1 Cor. 1:30). Defined in full at the close.
  • Rom. 3:22. "Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference" — "upon all": a robe placed on the believer from outside himself, without distinction of persons.
  • Rom. 3:24. "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" — FREELY: grace is the spring, the redemption in Christ the channel; nothing of the sinner's enters the price.
  • Rom. 3:25. "Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past" — the blood, laid hold of by faith, remits sins; and the remitting DECLARES God's righteousness rather than compromising it.
  • Rom. 3:26. "that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus" — the wonder of the gospel in one clause: God remains JUST — the law unbent — in the very act of justifying the believing sinner; mercy does not bend the law whose transgression is sin (see "What Sin Is — Transgression, Not Inheritance").
